subject_line: Three generations and the sealers of Kangaroo Island
email_body:
Dear Molly,

Heart of the Grass Tree gathers three generations of women on Kangaroo Island after a grandmother's death, while a second thread reaches back to the early European sealers and their contact with Ngarrindjeri people. I was curious how you decided to braid those two timelines, and whether your work as a poet shaped the way the island's landscape carries the story.

I'd also love to hear how managing Matilda Bookshop in the Adelaide Hills sits alongside your own writing.

book_title: Walking with Camels: The Story of Bertha Strehlow
subject_line: Giving voice to Bertha Strehlow in verse
email_body:
Dear Leni,

Walking with Camels tells Bertha Strehlow's story as a verse novel, and I understand it grew out of your doctorate, 'Giving Voice to Silence'. I'd be interested to hear how the move from research to poetry changed what you could say about Bertha, and why verse rather than prose felt right for her.

Your years in Mparntwe and your part in founding Ptilotus Press, now Running Waters Community Press, could also make a good thread.

subject_line: Openwork, limestone and a prairie childhood
email_body:
Dear Frances,

The title of Openwork and Limestone, your third poetry collection from Frontenac House, pairs something delicate and pierced with something solid and quarried. I wondered whether that tension speaks to the two landscapes in your life: the prairies where you grew up and the Lindenlea neighbourhood of Ottawa where you live now.

I'd also be curious how the move into longer fiction with your novel Skin Hunger has changed the way you work on poems.

subject_line: Suppressed history in The Speed of Mercy
email_body:
Dear Christy Ann,

The Speed of Mercy is framed around the cost of childhood betrayal and what happens when history is suppressed, and it unfolds in a rural Nova Scotia that only looks idyllic on the surface. Since you grew up in the Annapolis Valley, I'd love to know how much of that landscape and its silences fed the novel, and how your long interest in ghost stories shapes the way the past keeps surfacing in your fiction.

Dear Deirdre,

Few writers move as freely as you do between audiences: Adventures of an Island Cat Named Brupp for young readers, Afternoon Horses in poetry, and Darwin's Hornpipe, your novel for adults with Penumbra Press. I'd love to ask how you decide which form a story needs, and whether teaching the L.M. I'd be curious to hear what draws you to inhabit historical and legendary women, and how visual poetry and your recent books, Beast Body Epic and Genesis, push that work beyond the conventional page.

subject_line: An aging folk musician and the people around him
email_body:
Dear Stephanie,

Fallsy Downsies follows an aging folk musician and the people orbiting him, and it won the Dartmouth Book Award for Fiction. Homing, before it, set much of its story in the Spring Garden Road library, with a ghost among the cast. I'd love to hear how Halifax places find their way into your fiction, and how writing Amazing Atlantic Canadian Women with Penelope Jackson for young readers compared with the novel work, including the third novel you've been writing.

subject_line: Forty years of stories from the Alphorn Factory
email_body:
Dear Gary,

Scandal at the Alphorn Factory gathers forty years of your short fiction, from 1984 to 2024, and it went on to win the Hamilton Literary Award for Fiction, not long after Nothing the Same, Everything Haunted was the Hamilton Reads choice. I'd love to ask what it was like to reread your younger self while choosing those stories, and what you noticed changing in your sentences across four decades.

subject_line: After Five Wives: the turn toward Wild Hope
email_body:
Dear Joan,

Five Wives imagined the five women left behind in the Ecuadorian rainforest after their missionary husbands were killed. Wild Hope, which you launched in Winnipeg in 2023, has been described as a contemporary love story, a mystery and a piece of social criticism all at once. I'd be interested to hear how moving from a historical event to the present day changed the way you research and build a novel, and what Winnipeg gives you as a place to write from.

subject_line: Louise de Kiriline Lawrence and the songbirds of Pimisi Bay
email_body:
Dear Merilyn,

Woman, Watching follows Louise de Kiriline Lawrence and the songbirds of Pimisi Bay, and it made me think back to The Convict Lover, which also found its story in an overlooked life, there in Kingston. I'd love to ask what draws you to these real people at the edges of the record, and how you balance documentary research with the imaginative leaps of a biographer.

As founder of Kingston WritersFest, you might also have thoughts on the city's writing community.

subject_line: Delia Rabbit and a Queensland heatwave
email_body:
Dear Sophie,

The Rabbits sets Delia Rabbit, a former artist, inside a Queensland summer heatwave just as her middle son disappears, and it moves between magic realism and the pull of a crime story. I'd love to ask how you kept that balance between the uncanny and the suburban, and what Brisbane's heat gave the book that another setting couldn't. I'd also be curious how winning the Penguin Literary Prize with the manuscript shaped its path.

Dear Laurie,

I'd love to ask how you managed time on that scale, which years you chose to dwell on and which you let pass, and how writing about a family over decades has fed into the manuscript assessment work you now do for other writers.

subject_line: The free-diver who opens Well-Behaved Women
email_body:
Dear Emily,

Well-Behaved Women opens with "The sea also waits", about a free-diver who disappears during training, and closes with "The Woman at the Writers Festival". Between them, seventeen stories, many set in Western Australia, look at power, ageing, autonomy and what's expected of women. I'd love to ask how you chose that first and last story to frame the collection, and how your work reviewing and editing books has changed the way you read your own stories.
